paras: The Gillsburg lynching and reported riot was the hanging of an unnamed Black man by a posse at Gillsburg, a small town twelve miles northeast of Kentwood, Louisiana, on Sunday, November 15, 1903, after he was accused of assaulting a white woman. A wire dispatch from Kentwood added that Black residents who gathered in anger were met in a fight in which eighteen of them were killed, a figure it said was only "reported here tonight." The story ran in a handful of white papers in South Carolina, Kansas and Missouri; no confirmation, names or follow-up appear in the coverage.

According to the Kentwood special, a Black man was alleged to have assaulted a white woman on the evening of November 14, while the men of her family were absent, and then fled to the woods. Within minutes "fifty or more citizens" answered the alarm and began a manhunt with a description of the accused.

The posse searched the woods all night and found the man shortly before noon on Sunday. He was brought back to the village, where he was said to have been identified, and was hanged with a rope from the branch of a tree behind a barn. No officer is mentioned at the hanging.

The dispatch described the dead man as "popular with the members of his race" and said that Black villagers, angered by the lynching, gathered and that many of them were armed. In its words the Black residents "started the riot with the whites," and eighteen of them were reported killed and several others wounded. The sheriff and his deputies were said to have put down the riot.
None of the dead is named in any report, and no report of an inquest, arrests or a correction of the death toll was found.

All versions derive from one special from Kentwood, which the Watchman and Southron of Sumter, South Carolina, printed most fully under the headline "Negro Lynched for Usual Crime" and with the admission that "Details of the killing are very meagre." That paper described the gathered Black residents as "in an ugly mood" and "out looking for trouble," presenting the whites' account as fact. The Topeka State Journal and the Butler Weekly Times of Missouri ran a shorter text under the subhead "Louisiana Negroes Resented a Lynching."

The Newberry Herald and News reduced the story to one line in a news digest, and in the same column reported that an Illinois Central express had struck a train near Kentwood on Saturday night, killing twenty Black passengers. No account of the Gillsburg events was found in the Black press, so the story survives only in the white papers' versions of the wire.

The Kansas Agitator of Garnett placed the "race war" at Kentwood itself, dated it Monday, and alone said that "several whites" were wounded. The dispatch's November 15 dateline and its use of "today" support Sunday as the date. The wire itself located Gillsburg only by its distance from Kentwood, while the headlines and the Newberry digest called it "Gillsburg, La."

reader.title: Gillsburg lynching and reported riot
bases: The wire describes a posse hanging a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman, followed by a reported riot in which eighteen Black people were killed (A1, A3).

As reported, a posse of 'fifty or more' citizens hunted down and hanged, without any legal process, a Black man accused of assaulting a white woman (A1, A3); every element of the definition is present, but the account rests on a single unconfirmed Kentwood dispatch that names no one and calls its details 'very meagre' (A3).
Every version (A1, A2, A3, A5, A6) traces to one Kentwood special; no local paper, follow-up, correction or Black-press report confirms it.

accounts.label: Kentwood wire report
accounts.gist: A posse of fifty or more hanged the accused man; Black villagers, angered, gathered armed and 'started the riot with the whites', and eighteen of them were reported killed before the sheriff restored order.

accounts.label: Kansas Agitator rewrite
accounts.gist: A 'race war' at Kentwood on Monday in which both sides armed themselves; eighteen Black people killed and several whites wounded.

framing.detail: The Watchman and Southron headlined 'Negro Lynched for Usual Crime' and described the Black villagers as 'in an ugly mood' and 'out looking for trouble'.
Kansas and Missouri papers ran the dispatch as '18 Killed in Riot' and 'Eighteen Dead in a Riot', with the subhead 'Louisiana Negroes Resented a Lynching'.
The Newberry Herald and News gave it one line in a news digest, stating the assault as fact.

versions.value: Sunday, Nov. 15 ('today' in the Nov. 15 dispatch; 'on Sunday')

conflicts.note: The Nov. 15 dateline and 'today' in the fullest text favor Sunday; the Kansas Agitator brief is a later rewrite.

versions.value: Gillsburg, twelve miles northeast of Kentwood, La.; headlined 'Gillsburg, La.'

conflicts.note: A railroad-wreck casualty list in a Mississippi paper (A4, another episode) gives a passenger's home as 'Gillsburg, Miss.', so the state in the headlines may be wrong; the wire itself names only the distance from Kentwood.

versions.value: Only Black people reported wounded ('Several others were wounded')

conflicts.note: The white wounded appear only in the rewritten Kansas brief.

record_check.dossier: The dispatches say 'Gillsburg, La.' / twelve miles northeast of Kentwood, La.; only an unrelated wreck list (A4) gives 'Gillsburg, Miss.' State should be marked uncertain or sourced.
